product.title: Slovenian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Slovenian: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Slovenian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up — from dvojina (a special form for exactly two people, which has all but vanished from the world's languages) to the six cases that do the work of prepositions.

blocks.text: Slovenian is spoken by about two million people — roughly the population of Houston. That number usually makes people ask: why learn it? The answer lies in the number itself. In a country as small as Slovenia, a foreigner who can say one whole sentence in their language isn't ordinary; it's an event. You'll feel it from your very first sentence.

But there's an even more interesting reason. Slovenian keeps an antique that has died out almost everywhere else in the world: **dvojina**, the dual — a special form for **exactly two**. Ancient Greek had it, Sanskrit had it, Arabic still has traces of it. In modern Europe, only Slovenian uses it every day, in every verb, every noun, every adjective.

This means *midva sva* (we two are) is not a fancy variant of *mi smo* (we are). It's obligatory: if there are two of you, saying *mi smo* sounds wrong, like saying "all three of us" about two people. Slovenians even joke that theirs is the only language with a grammar made especially for couples in love.

The good news is that three things are **missing** in Slovenian, and they're three of the things that torment learners of European languages most. **There are no articles** — no *a/the*, no *der/die/das*, no *le/la*. *Knjiga* can mean "book", "a book", or "the book"; context decides. **The spelling is honest** — twenty-five letters, one letter one sound, no silent letters. And **there are no tones**, and only two or three sounds that English speakers don't already make.

So Slovenian does have difficulties, but they're neatly gathered in just four places: **the dual**, **six cases** (endings that do the work of prepositions), **three noun genders**, and **the order of little words** — *sem*, *se*, *ga* — that always sit in the second seat of the sentence.

That's why none of the four is put off to the back of the book. The dual is installed in unit 3, cases start seeping in from unit 2 and get units of their own in units 6 and 8, and the stubborn little words are covered in unit 11 — right when you start building longer sentences.
The explanations are short on purpose. What's long isn't the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 minutes without distractions, not two hours chopped into pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.

Read aloud. In Slovenian it costs little: the spelling is almost completely honest, so once you know the twenty-five letters and their sounds, you can read any word — including ones you've never seen.

From the first unit, get into the habit of asking **how many people** before choosing a verb form. One, two, or three or more — that question never stops mattering in Slovenian, and the habit of asking it is what separates fluent beginners from halting ones.

Don't wait until your accent is perfect before you dare to speak. Slovenians almost never meet foreigners willing to learn their language; even the smallest effort is welcomed far more warmly than you'd imagine.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Veliko sreče!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same structure, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Slovenian aloud, without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most, yet it's where you see how Slovenian *thinks*. Example: *Kako ti je ime?* literally means "how to-you is name?", not "what is your name".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with a pronunciation guide.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From unit 3 on, the last exercise in each unit sends you back to a unit you've already done — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. It works in reverse: cover the Slovenian, look at the English, then rebuild the Slovenian sentence from memory.
This is the part that turns "I once understood it" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit unique to this course
items: Every time you meet a new noun, say it together with a preposition: *šola* → *v šoli*, *miza* → *na mizi*, *Ljubljana* → *v Ljubljani*. Ten seconds per word, and cases stop being theory.

And every time you mention people, count first. One? Two? Three or more? Slovenian demands that answer before it lets you choose a verb, so it's better for the question to become a reflex now than later.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Slovenian spelling rewards that generously — with one exception you need to know from the start, and that's what the next page is about.

The Slovenian alphabet has **twenty-five letters**: a b c č d e f g h i j k l m n o p r s š t u v z ž. There's no *q*, *w*, *x*, or *y*. There are no silent letters. Almost every letter is read exactly as written — and the ones that aren't all fit on this one page.

The **Say it** column throughout this course uses English-friendly spelling, with CAPITAL LETTERS marking the stressed syllable. The capitals matter: unlike Czech or Hungarian, Slovenian stress is **not always at the front**. *Ljubljána* is stressed in the middle, *slovénščina* in the middle, *tržníca* at the end. There's no rule — so learn the stress along with the word, just as you learn its sounds.

blocks.text: Watch the pair **c** and **č**: the one without a hat is *ts*, the one with a hat is *ch*. English speakers instinctively read *c* as "k" or "s", and it trips them up again and again until it finally sticks. *Cena* = TSAY-nah (price), *čevelj* = CHAY-vuhly (shoe).
One big exception: l and v that turn into u

This is the one place where Slovenian spelling lies, and it lies very diligently. **The letters *l* and *v* at the end of a syllable are said like *u*** (a short *w* glide). Not sometimes — almost always.

This rule becomes very important from unit 12 on, because **every Slovenian past tense ends in *-l***: *delal, pil, bral, šel*. If you say "deh-lahl", Slovenians will understand you, but you'll sound like you're spelling. Say **DAY-low**, and you instantly sound much closer.

The preposition **v** (in, to) stands alone with no vowel, and it attaches to the next word as a *u* sound: *v Ljubljani* is said **oo-lyoob-LYAH-nee**, *v šoli* is said **oo-SHOH-lee**. The same goes for **z** and **s** (with): both attach with no pause.
Vowels: three kinds of e, two kinds of o
*a*, *i*, and *u* are always **ah**, **ee**, **oo** (*father*, *see*, *food*). Only *e* and *o* branch out, and this course spells them like this in the Say it column:

head: Spelled
Sound
Example
rows: closed e — like *ay* in **say**, but without sliding off
closed o — like *o* in **go**, but pure

blocks.title: Words with no vowels at all
items: Slovenian has words like *vrt* (garden), *prst* (finger), *trg* (square), *krt* (mole). The vowel isn't written — but it's there, and it sounds exactly like the **schwa** (*uh*), slipped in **before** the *r*.
*vrt* is said **vuhrt**, *prst* is said **puhrst**, *trg* is said **tuhrg**, *Trst* (Trieste) is said **tuhrst**. If you can say the *u* in "fur", you can already say all of them.

blocks.text: Voiced letters that go quiet at the end of a word

At the end of a word, voiced letters turn into their voiceless partners: *b*→p, *d*→t, *g*→k, *z*→s, *ž*→sh. So *grad* (castle) is said **graht**, *Bog* (God) is said **bohk**, *mož* (husband) is said **mohsh**, *nož* (knife) is said **nohsh**. The spelling stays the same — the change happens only in your mouth. (German does exactly the same.)
And that's it. Nothing else. Read the first ten words of unit 1 aloud, and this page will stop feeling like a list of rules.
Among learners, the reputation of the Slavic languages rests on one word: **cases**. Before you begin unit 1, it's worth knowing what you **don't** have to do — the list is longer than people expect.

items: **No articles.** *Knjiga* = book, a book, or the book. English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish all make you choose; Slovenian doesn't.
**No continuous forms.** *Berem* means "I read" and "I'm reading" at the same time. No *am reading* versus *read*.
**Subject pronouns can be dropped.** The verb ending already tells you who's acting: *berem* can only be "I read". *Jaz* is used when you want emphasis.
**No tones, no new script.** The same Latin letters, plus three hats: č, š, ž.
**Word order is flexible.** *Anna bere knjigo* and *Knjigo bere Anna* are both correct; only the emphasis shifts — a bit like "Anna is reading the book" versus "The book, Anna is reading".

English and Slovenian both absorbed the same waves of international European words, much of it from Latin and Greek. The result is several hundred words you'll simply recognize:

Look at *restavracija*: the *v* in the middle is said as *u*, so it sounds like **rays-tow-RAH-tsee-yah** — close to "restoration". Once the *l/v* → *u* rule sticks, words like this open up on their own.
What you do have to work on
To be honest, here's a short list of what can't be avoided. All of it is installed gradually in this course; nothing is thrown at you all at once:

blocks.text: Six rows. That's all the difficulty Slovenian holds at A1, and the twenty units ahead are a way of installing all six slowly, until they stop feeling like a list.
These pages aren't study material — they're a place for a quick look when you forget a form in the middle of an exercise. Everything here has already been explained slowly in its own unit.
1. Biti — three number lanes (units 1, 3)
2. Verb endings — one list for everything
3. The six cases (units 2, 6, 7, 8, 15, 18)

blocks.text: Only four are truly essential at A1: the basic form, the **tožilnik** (Accusative: *Pijem kavo*), the **mestnik** (Locative: *V Ljubljani*), and the **rodilnik** (Genitive: *Nimam časa*, *pet knjig*).
4. Four patterns for number + noun (unit 5)
What decides is the **last number** spoken: *enaindvajset knjiga* goes back to the singular, because 21 ends in "one".
5. Three tenses (units 11, 12, 17)

The *-l* ending follows the subject: **-l** one man, **-la** one woman or two men, **-li** two women or three or more, **-le** three or more women, **-lo** for things with no gender. And remember: that ending is always said like **u** — *delal* = DAY-low.
6. Adjectives and possessives
7. Naslonke — the order in the second seat (unit 11)
The order is fixed: **bi → sem/si/je → se → mi/ti/mu → me/te/ga/jo**. They all sit after the first word or phrase. *Ime **mi je** Budi.* *Zbudil **sem se** ob šestih.* *Danes **se mi** mudi.*
8. Negation
The forty verbs below cover most everyday conversation. The third column is the "I" form, which can't always be guessed from the dictionary form — learn both together.
Women add **-a** to the fourth column: *bila*, *šla*, *rekla*, *delala*. For two people and for three or more, use *-la*, *-li*, or *-le* as in the table on the previous page.

And remember aspect from unit 14: almost every verb on this list has a twin in the finished form — *kuhati/skuhati*, *pisati/napisati*, *brati/prebrati*, *jesti/pojesti*. When in doubt, use the form on this list; it's more general and never misunderstood.
**Srečno — in se slišimo!**
